lesson.title: Run: The Horizontal Half of Slope
lesson.summary: Run is the horizontal change between two points on a line, calculated by subtracting their x-coordinates, and it forms the denominator of the slope ratio.
lesson.body:
If rise measures how far a line climbs vertically between two points, run measures how far it travels horizontally over that same stretch. Between two points on a line, (x1, y1) and (x2, y2), the run is calculated as x2 - x1, the difference between their x-coordinates. This is the denominator of the slope formula, matching rise as the numerator, and together the two values rebuild the full ratio that defines a line's steepness once both pieces are known. Just as rise mirrors the y-coordinate, run mirrors the x-coordinate, so the same subtraction pattern, second point minus first point, is used for both, keeping the two calculations consistent with one another.

The sign of the run indicates direction along the horizontal axis. A positive run means the second point sits to the right of the first, and a negative run means it sits to the left. A run of zero would mean both points share the same x-coordinate, which happens along a perfectly vertical line, a case where slope is undefined because dividing by a run of zero is not a valid operation in ordinary arithmetic, no matter what the rise happens to be.

Here is a worked example that finishes the calculation started in the previous chapter. Using the same two points on the line y = 3x - 2, namely (-1, -5) and (3, 7), calculate the run going from the first point to the second: run = x2 - x1 = 3 - (-1) = 3 + 1 = 4. So moving from (-1, -5) to (3, 7), the line travels 4 units horizontally, a much smaller distance than the 12 units of rise found previously.

Now the rise and run from these same two points can be combined into the slope ratio: slope = rise divided by run = 12 divided by 4 = 3. This matches the slope of 3 already found earlier using different pairs of points on this same line, (0, -2) and (2, 4), and again using (1, 1) and (2, 4). Three separate pairs of points, each producing a rise and run of its own, all reduce to the identical slope value of 3, which is exactly the guarantee that makes a line straight: the ratio of vertical change to horizontal change never varies, no matter which two points are chosen to measure it.

Rise and run together give a concrete, countable way to picture slope: starting at any point on a line, rise tells you how many units to move up or down, and run tells you how many units to move right or left, and moving by that exact combination lands you back on the line at another valid point. This rise-over-run picture is often the fastest way to sketch a line by hand once its slope and one point are already known, without needing to calculate any additional ordered pairs first. Starting from the y-intercept (0, -2) on this same line and applying a rise of 3 and a run of 1 repeatedly traces out the exact points (1, 1), (2, 4), and (3, 7) already found in earlier chapters, one step at a time.
